title: Stand Firm in Faith: The Sign of Immanuel
summary: When the kings of Aram and Israel march against Jerusalem, King Ahaz and his people tremble. Isaiah meets Ahaz with his son Shear-jashub and tells him to be calm, for the plot will fail, but warns that if he does not stand firm in faith he will not stand at all. Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign, so the Lord gives one anyway: the virgin (or young woman) will bear a son named Immanuel, and before the boy is old enough to choose good and reject evil, the lands of the two kings Ahaz fears will be laid waste. But Assyria, the power Ahaz is courting, will come as God's hired razor and leave Judah's own fields to briers and thorns.
story:
Chapter 6 told of Isaiah's call to speak to a people who would not listen. Chapter 7 shows that commission in action, as Isaiah speaks to the king himself. This chapter begins a section (roughly 7:1 to 12:6) sometimes called the Book of Immanuel, which moves from Ahaz's unbelief to promises of a child and a king who will rule in justice. The house of David, to whom God promised an everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7), is represented by a frightened king who would rather trust Assyria than God.

The chapter is also the first half of a deliberate pair. The meeting place in verse 3, the conduit of the upper pool on the road to the Launderer's Field, is exactly where the Assyrian envoy will stand to demand Jerusalem's surrender in 36:2, a generation later. There Ahaz's son Hezekiah will do what Ahaz refused to do: spread the threat before the LORD and trust him (37:14-20). Between these two kings the whole of Isaiah 1 to 39 turns on a single question: in whom will David's house trust? The Immanuel sign stands at the center of the first crisis, offering both reassurance and warning, and it sets up the promises of chapters 8, 9, and 11.
historical:
The setting is the Syro-Ephraimite war of about 734 to 732 BC (the name joins Syria, that is Aram, and Ephraim, the leading tribe of the northern kingdom of Israel). Rezin king of Aram, ruling from Damascus, and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel, ruling from Samaria, were organizing resistance to Assyria and tried to force Judah to join. When Ahaz refused, they invaded to replace him with a puppet king, the son of Tabeal (verse 6). That man is otherwise unknown; W. F. Albright (Bulletin of the American Schools of Oriental Research 140, 1955) connected the name with a Tabeel district east of the Jordan and suggested the pretender may have had a claim through the royal family. Second Kings 15:37 to 16:9 and 2 Chronicles 28:5-21 tell the same story from the side of the royal annals; 2 Kings 16:5 is nearly word for word the same as verse 1. Against Isaiah's counsel, Ahaz sent silver and gold from the temple and the palace treasuries to Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria (reigned 745 to 727 BC) with the message, “I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me from the hands of the kings of Aram and Israel, who are rising up against me” (2 Kings 16:7).

Assyria's own records confirm the outline. The Assyrian eponym list, which names each year after an official and notes the king's campaign, records a march ‘to Philistia’ in 734 and campaigns against Damascus in the next two years. A summary inscription of Tiglath-pileser on a clay tablet in the British Museum (K 3751, often called Summary Inscription 7) lists among the western kings who brought tribute ‘Jehoahaz of Judah’, the full form of Ahaz's name, beside the kings of Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Ashkelon. Other texts of the same king record that he received tribute from Rezin, later besieged Damascus, and after the Israelites overthrew Pekah installed Hoshea in his place, matching 2 Kings 15:29-30 and 16:9. Damascus fell in 732 BC and Rezin was executed; Galilee and Gilead were annexed as Assyrian provinces; within about ten years Samaria itself fell (722 BC).

The sixty-five years of verse 8 are harder to explain. Counting from about 734 BC, sixty-five years reach the end of the reign of Esarhaddon (681 to 669 BC), and Ezra 4:2 records foreigners in the land of Samaria who said Esarhaddon had brought them there, while Ezra 4:10 credits the deportations to a later king, Osnappar (usually identified with Ashurbanipal). Many interpreters therefore take the figure as pointing to the final resettlement of the north, after which Ephraim no longer existed as a people. Others, noting that the clause interrupts the neat parallel of verses 8a and 9a, regard it as a later explanatory addition.

The chronology of Ahaz's family matters for the interpretation of verse 14. Second Kings 16:2 says Ahaz was twenty when he began to reign and reigned sixteen years; 2 Kings 18:2 says his son Hezekiah was twenty-five when he succeeded him. Taken at face value, these figures mean Hezekiah was already born before Ahaz became king, which is why several medieval Jewish commentators rejected the identification of Immanuel with Hezekiah. Precise dates for Ahaz's reign differ by a few years between the standard chronologies of the kings.
cultural:
Isaiah meets Ahaz at the end of the conduit of the upper pool (verse 3), probably because the king was inspecting Jerusalem's water supply in preparation for siege. Water was a city's lifeline in war, and Jerusalem's main source, the Gihon spring, lay outside the eastern wall; a generation later Hezekiah would cut his tunnel to bring its water inside (2 Kings 20:20, 2 Chronicles 32:30). The exact location of the upper pool is unknown. Isaiah brings his son, whose name, Shear-jashub, means ‘a remnant will return’, a walking message that carried both threat (only a remnant) and promise (a remnant will return). Isaiah later says that he and his children are signs in Israel (8:18). Names as signs were an established prophetic practice; Hosea's children bore similar names (Hosea 1), and Isaiah's second son will be named Maher-shalal-hash-baz, ‘swift to the spoil, quick to the plunder’ (8:1-4).

Kings in the ancient Near East consulted the gods before war. Assyrian kings kept diviners who read the livers of sacrificed sheep and the movements of the stars, and asked specific yes-or-no questions about campaigns. Israel was forbidden divination (Deuteronomy 18:10-14), but the LORD sometimes gave a sign to confirm his word, to Moses (Exodus 3:12, 4:1-9), to Gideon (Judges 6:36-40), and later to Hezekiah (Isaiah 38:7-8). So the offer of verse 11, a sign as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven, was extraordinary but not strange. Ahaz's refusal borrows the language of Deuteronomy 6:16, which forbids putting the LORD to the test, but testing God meant demanding proof in unbelief, as Israel did at Massah (Exodus 17:7). Refusing a sign God himself offers is the opposite of reverence. The refusal masks a decision already made to trust Assyria, and it is the house of David, not only Ahaz, that Isaiah then addresses.

The last verses picture the land after invasion. Curds and honey (verses 15 and 22) could be the food of plenty, as in the land flowing with milk and honey, but here they are the diet of a few survivors in a land whose fields have gone wild: milk from the one heifer and two sheep a man keeps, and honey from wild bees. Vineyards were Judah's most valuable farmland, planted on terraced hillsides that had to be hoed by hand; a price of a shekel of silver a vine (verse 23) marks the best land. Shaving the head, the body, and the beard (verse 20) was a deep humiliation inflicted on captives and enemies, which is why Hanun's shaving of David's envoys started a war (2 Samuel 10:4-6). The razor is ‘hired’, a stinging reminder that Ahaz had just hired Assyria with temple silver.
literary:
The chapter is prose narrative with embedded oracles. It falls into two encounters with Ahaz (verses 1 to 9 and 10 to 17), each built around a prophetic word, followed by four short oracles introduced by ‘on that day’ (verses 18 and 19, 20, 21 and 22, 23 to 25) describing Assyria's devastation. Verse 1 tells the outcome in advance (the kings could not take Jerusalem), so the suspense lies not in whether the city falls but in whether the king will believe.

The first encounter builds an argument from pattern. The heads of Aram and Ephraim are named in verses 8 and 9 (Damascus and Rezin, Samaria and the son of Remaliah), and the missing line, Judah's head, is left for Ahaz to supply: the LORD. The oracle closes with one of the most famous wordplays in the Bible, built on the root aman, to be firm or to believe: roughly, if you do not firm up in faith, you will not be made firm at all. The same root gives amen and the Niphal verb of the promise to David in 2 Samuel 7:16, “Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me”, so the wordplay reminds the dynasty of the promise it is being asked to lean on. The verbs are plural, addressed to the whole royal house.

The second encounter pivots on Ahaz's refusal and on a telling shift in pronouns. In verse 11 Isaiah speaks of “the LORD your God”; in verse 13, after the refusal, he says “my God”. The address becomes plural, “O house of David”, and the sign of verse 14 is given to that house. The sign itself uses a traditional birth-announcement formula (behold, a woman pregnant and bearing a son, and she will call his name), the same pattern used to Hagar (Genesis 16:11) and to Manoah's wife (Judges 13:5), and it cuts both ways: deliverance from Rezin and Pekah within a few years, and in the same lifetime the worst days since the kingdom split. The name Immanuel returns in 8:8 and 8:10, binding chapters 7 and 8, and the child grows through chapter 9 into the royal son with divine titles and in chapter 11 into the shoot of Jesse. The four closing oracles are held together by repeated images: insects that come at God's whistle, a hired razor, a remnant eating curds and honey, and the refrain of briers and thorns, which ties this chapter to the ruined vineyard of 5:6.

outline.t: Isaiah meets Ahaz: stand firm in faith
Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign
Four oracles of the coming devastation

doctrines.note: Verse 9 is one of the Old Testament's clearest statements about faith: to believe God is to stand, and not to believe is to fall. Faith here is not a feeling or an opinion but reliance on God's promise to David in a real political crisis, instead of on the power one can hire. Isaiah will state the same principle in 28:16, “the one who believes will never be shaken”.

Verse 14 is the classic test case for how prophecy and fulfillment relate. Readers divide over whether it is direct prediction, a sign for Ahaz's day that Matthew sees filled out in Jesus, or both, and the chapter shows that a prophetic sign can carry near and far horizons at once.

The sign of Immanuel is given to the house of David at the moment its king has failed. The child who bears the name is tied in the following chapters to the land (8:8) and to the royal son whose government has no end (9:6-7), so the hope for David's line passes from Ahaz to a child God himself provides.

Isaiah's first hearers heard in Immanuel, God with us, a promise of God's saving presence with Judah. Matthew 1:23 hears it as a statement of who Jesus is, God come to be with his people in human flesh, and the church confesses that in him the name became a description.

God controls the outcome: the plot of Aram and Israel “will not arise; it will not happen” (verse 7), and Assyria, whom Ahaz hires as a savior, comes when the LORD whistles and serves as his razor. The powers of the world serve God's purposes even when they do not know it.

words.note: Almah, translated virgin in the BSB, KJV, NIV, and ESV and young woman in the RSV, NRSV, and the Jewish Publication Society's translation. It occurs seven times in the Hebrew Bible (Genesis 24:43, Exodus 2:8, Psalm 68:25, Proverbs 30:19, Song of Solomon 1:3 and 6:8, and here). The standard lexicons give the sense of a young woman of marriageable age, a girl ripe for marriage. In the places where the context is clear she is unmarried (Rebekah at the well, Miriam as a girl), and the word is never clearly used of a married woman, though Proverbs 30:19 is debated. The more specific word for a virgin is betulah, which itself sometimes needs a clarifying phrase (Genesis 24:16). The debate over this one word is set out under the hard questions.

Immanuel, ‘God with us’, from immanu (with us) and El (God). It occurs as a name only here and in 8:8, and the same words stand as a cry of confidence in 8:10, “For God is with us.” It can be heard as a statement of faith (God is with us) or as a description of the child who embodies it. Matthew 1:23 translates it and applies it to Jesus, and Matthew's Gospel closes with the risen Jesus promising to be with his disciples always (28:20), framing the whole book with the name.

Aman, to be firm, reliable, or (in the Hiphil) to believe, occurring a little over a hundred times, fifteen of them in Isaiah. In the Niphal it means to be made firm or established, and it describes the enduring house promised to David (2 Samuel 7:16), a faithful servant, and water that is assured (33:16). In the Hiphil it means to lean one's weight on something firm, as “Abram believed the LORD” (Genesis 15:6). Verse 9 uses both stems for its wordplay, and the same root gives amen and emunah, faithfulness. Faith in this vocabulary is not a leap in the dark but standing on ground that holds.

Ot, sign, about eighty times in the Old Testament, eleven of them in Isaiah. A sign confirms God's word, sometimes by a wonder (the plagues of Egypt, the shadow on Hezekiah's stairway in 38:7-8), sometimes by something ordinary given meaning (the rainbow in Genesis 9:12-13, circumcision in Genesis 17:11, a name, a child). Some signs precede their fulfillment, and some, like the sign to Moses in Exodus 3:12, can only be recognized after the event. Ahaz refuses to ask, and God gives a sign anyway, one that confirms both his protection and his judgment.

Nasah, to test or try, occurring about thirty-six times. It is used of God testing his people to reveal what is in their hearts (Genesis 22:1, Deuteronomy 8:2) and of people testing God by demanding that he prove himself (Exodus 17:2 and 7, Psalm 78:18). Deuteronomy 6:16 forbids the second. Ahaz uses the verb to decline God's offer, borrowing the law's words for the opposite of the law's purpose: refusing a sign God has offered is not humility but evasion.

Shaqat, to be quiet, still, or at rest, about forty times, seven in Isaiah. In Judges it describes the land at rest after a deliverer's victory (Judges 3:11), and Isaiah uses it for the quiet trust he urges on the kings of Judah. The Hiphil imperative in verse 4, ‘show quietness’, is paired with a command to take care and not fear. Isaiah 30:15 states the same counsel to a later king: “your strength would lie in quiet confidence”. Quietness here is not passivity but the calm of someone whose security rests on God rather than on alliances.

Shear-jashub, ‘a remnant will return’, the name of Isaiah's son, found only in verse 3. Its two words carry Isaiah's double message: shear, remnant, speaks of loss (only a remnant), and yashuv, will return, uses shuv, the ordinary Hebrew verb for coming back and for repenting. Isaiah 10:20-22 plays on the name directly: a remnant will return to the Mighty God, though Israel be as the sand of the sea. The boy stands beside his father as a living sermon while Isaiah speaks to the king.

christ:
Matthew 1:22-23 quotes verse 14 from its Greek form: “Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”). Matthew's narrative first reports that Mary's child is conceived by the Holy Spirit (1:18-20), and then reads Isaiah's sign as answering to that event. He makes two changes to the Greek. The Septuagint has ‘you will call’, addressed to Ahaz or the house of David; Matthew writes ‘they will call’, so the name becomes the confession of the people who receive the child. And he adds the translation, because the name now describes the child: in Jesus, God is with us. Matthew's Gospel then ends with the risen Jesus promising, “surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (28:20), forming a frame around the whole book.

Matthew does not read verse 14 in isolation. The chapter's sign is given to the house of David when its king had failed, and within Isaiah the child grows into a larger figure: Immanuel is the owner of the land that Assyria floods (8:8), the royal son whose names include Mighty God and whose kingdom has no end (9:6-7), and the shoot from Jesse's stump on whom the Spirit rests (11:1-2). Matthew's genealogy, which traces Jesus through Ahaz and Hezekiah (1:9), makes the point that the promise to David survived its worst kings. Luke tells the same conception independently (Luke 1:26-38) without citing Isaiah, though Gabriel's words to Mary echo the birth formula of this verse.

The chapter's other great line also reaches the New Testament. The call to stand firm in faith in verse 9 belongs with Isaiah 28:16, the cornerstone laid in Zion on which the one who believes will not be shaken, which Paul and Peter apply to Christ (Romans 9:33, 1 Peter 2:6). Ahaz is the pattern of the unbelief that seeks security anywhere but in God's promise; the child is God's answer to that unbelief. The church confesses that in Jesus the name Immanuel is not only a hope but a fact: God is truly with us, fully God and fully human.
interpretation:
The reading of verse 14 divided Jews and Christians very early. The Septuagint, the Greek translation made by Jews in Egypt before the Christian era, rendered almah with parthenos, usually ‘virgin’, and Matthew quotes it. In the second century AD the Jewish Greek translators Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion chose neanis, ‘young woman’, and Justin Martyr's Dialogue with Trypho (around 155 to 160) records the debate: Trypho reads neanis and applies the prophecy to Hezekiah (chapters 43, 67, and 71). Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.21.1) objects to the renderings of Aquila and Theodotion, and Origen (Against Celsus 1.34-35) argues that a young woman bearing a child in the ordinary way could hardly be called a sign given by the Lord himself. Jerome, in his commentary on Isaiah (about 408 to 410), argued that almah meant a young woman kept secluded, and so more than a virgin. Verse 9 had its own history: the Old Latin, following the Greek, read ‘unless you believe, you will not understand’, and Augustine made the line a principle of Christian thought in On the Trinity 15.2, Letter 120, and Sermon 43; Anselm's Proslogion (1078) closes its first chapter with the same thought.

Medieval Jewish commentators kept the sign in Ahaz's day. Rashi identified the young woman with Isaiah's wife, the prophetess of 8:3, and rejected the Hezekiah reading because, counting the years of the kings, Hezekiah was born before Ahaz began to reign; Abraham Ibn Ezra rejected Hezekiah for the same reason. Luther, answering a rumor that he denied Mary's virginity, argued in That Jesus Christ Was Born a Jew (1523) that almah suited Isaiah's meaning better than betulah because it joins virginity with youth and readiness for marriage. Calvin's commentary on Isaiah (from his lectures, 1551, revised 1559) insisted that the sign must be something extraordinary and read it directly of Christ.

Modern scholarship remains divided. E. J. Young (1965) and J. Alec Motyer (The Prophecy of Isaiah, 1993) defend a direct prophecy of the Messiah's virginal conception; Raymond E. Brown (The Birth of the Messiah, 1977) argued that Isaiah meant a child of his own day and that Matthew read the Greek text in the light of what the church believed about Jesus' conception. When the Revised Standard Version (1952) printed ‘young woman’ with ‘virgin’ in a footnote, one pastor, M. Luther Hux, publicly burned the page; ‘young woman’ has since become standard in the NRSV and the Jewish Publication Society's translation, while the NIV, ESV, and BSB keep ‘virgin’.

In worship the chapter belongs to Advent and the Annunciation. The last of the great ‘O’ antiphons sung before Christmas in the Western church, O Emmanuel, gathers its titles, and the Latin hymn built on those antiphons became, in John Mason Neale's translation of 1851, the hymn now sung as O Come, O Come, Emmanuel. The Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 10 to 16 with Matthew 1:18-25 on the Fourth Sunday of Advent in Year A, and verses 10 to 14 on the feast of the Annunciation (March 25). Handel's Messiah (1742) sets the verse as a short alto recitative in Part One. In the Catacomb of Priscilla in Rome a third-century fresco shows a mother and child beside a man pointing to a star; he is usually identified as Balaam (Numbers 24:17), though some have seen Isaiah.
text:
English Bibles differ most visibly in verse 14. The Masoretic Text reads haalmah, ‘the young woman’, with the article; the Septuagint has he parthenos, ‘the virgin’; the second-century Jewish revisions of the Greek (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion) have neanis, ‘young woman’. The KJV, NIV, ESV, and BSB translate ‘virgin’; the RSV, NRSV, and the Jewish Publication Society's translation have ‘young woman’. The Hebrew harah is an adjective, not a verb, so it can mean ‘is pregnant’ or ‘will be pregnant’, which is why some versions read ‘is with child’ (NRSV) and others ‘will conceive’ (KJV, ESV). The verb for naming also varies: the Masoretic Text reads a form usually taken as ‘and she will call’; the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (1QIsaa, copied about 125 BC) reads a form most scholars take as ‘and he will call’ or ‘and one will call’; the Septuagint has ‘you will call’; Matthew has ‘they will call’.

Verse 9's wordplay does not survive in the Septuagint, which reads ‘if you do not believe, neither will you understand’, and through the Old Latin that reading shaped Augustine and the medieval church. In verse 11 the Hebrew consonants read as ‘to Sheol’ (the realm of the dead, balancing ‘heaven’) by the ancient versions and most modern Bibles can also be pointed as an imperative, ‘ask it’; the difference does not change the sense of an unlimited offer. In verse 6 the Masoretic vowels give the pretender's father the name Taveal, which sounds like ‘good for nothing’, where many scholars think the name was Tavel, ‘God is good’; English Bibles vary between Tabeal and Tabeel. Many critical commentators regard the time note of verse 8b (sixty-five years) and the words ‘the king of Assyria’ at the end of verses 17 and 20 as later explanatory additions, though no manuscript lacks them. The chapter and verse numbering is the same in Hebrew and English Bibles.

teach.big: When fear drives God's people to look for security in the power they can hire, God calls them to stand firm on his promise, and he gives his own sign, a child named God with us, that outlasts the unbelief of kings.

outline.t: Fear is real and it shakes whole communities, but verse 1 tells us the outcome first: the question is not whether God can save but whether we will trust him.
God meets us at the place of our practical fears, names the threat for what it is (smoldering stubs, not a firestorm), and calls for quietness before action.
God's word outlasts every human plan, and faith means leaning our weight on his promise; there is no other ground that holds.
Unbelief can wear the clothes of piety: Ahaz quotes Scripture to refuse the God who gave it, and wears out God's patience as well as man's.
God gives his own sign to a failing royal house, a child named God with us, which brings both rescue from the present threat and judgment through the ally Ahaz chose.
The security we buy apart from God becomes the instrument of our loss: the hired razor, the emptied fields, and a remnant living on what the wild land gives.

teach.pitfalls:
The first pitfall is to lift verse 14 out of the chapter and preach it only at Christmas, as if Ahaz, Rezin, and Assyria were scenery. Matthew's reading is richer when the congregation sees the dark setting in which God first gave the sign: a frightened king, a failing dynasty, and a God who keeps his promise to David anyway. The second is to treat the almah debate as a test of orthodoxy in either direction. The church's confession of the virginal conception rests on the Gospel accounts in Matthew 1 and Luke 1, and faithful scholars differ on how directly Isaiah's words predicted it; teachers should state the options fairly rather than suggest that anyone who translates ‘young woman’ denies the virgin birth.

A third pitfall is to turn verse 9 into a promise that faith guarantees political or personal success. Isaiah's word to Ahaz was that the Aramean and Israelite threat would fail, but he also foretold that Judah would suffer terribly from Assyria; standing firm in faith meant trusting God's promise to David through the judgment, not escaping all loss. A fourth is to treat Ahaz's refusal as admirable modesty. The text plainly treats it as unbelief: God had offered the sign, and declining it was a way of keeping a door open to Assyria. Finally, avoid allegorizing the flies, bees, and razor. They are vivid pictures of Egypt and Assyria as God's instruments, and the point is that the empires Judah feared or courted are under his command.
teach.pastoral: This chapter speaks directly to anxious people, and especially to those who make decisions under pressure: parents, leaders, anyone whose heart has shaken “like trees in the forest shaken by the wind”. Teach Isaiah's first words, calm down and do not be afraid, as God's gentleness before any rebuke. At the same time, be careful not to shame people who struggle with anxiety or who take practical steps to protect themselves; Isaiah did not condemn Ahaz for inspecting the water supply but for trusting Assyria instead of God. For those who feel that their family or leaders have failed them, the chapter offers real comfort: God's promise did not depend on Ahaz, and the sign was given precisely when the king had failed.

hard.q: Does Isaiah 7:14 predict a virgin birth, or did Matthew misread a sign meant for Ahaz?
hard.a:
The objection is old and serious. The Hebrew almah means a young woman of marriageable age, not specifically a virgin; the word for a virgin in the strict sense is betulah. The adjective harah can mean ‘is pregnant’, suggesting a woman already with child in Ahaz's day. Verses 15 and 16 tie the sign to a timetable of a few years: before the boy can tell good from evil, the lands of Rezin and Pekah will be deserted, which happened by 732 BC. On this reading the sign concerned a child born then, perhaps to the king's household or to Isaiah (compare 8:3-4 and 8:18). Trypho, in Justin Martyr's Dialogue, applied the verse to Hezekiah; Rashi applied it to Isaiah's wife and son; modern Jewish scholarship and many Christian critical scholars, such as Raymond E. Brown (The Birth of the Messiah, 1977), agree that Isaiah spoke of a child of his own time. The skeptic Thomas Paine, in The Age of Reason (Part II, 1795), made the same case more sharply, arguing that the verse had no more to do with Jesus than with anyone else and that Christian translators had changed ‘young woman’ into ‘virgin’. Jewish readers add that Matthew's argument depends on the Greek parthenos rather than the Hebrew.

Christian responses fall into three main groups. Some argue that the verse directly predicts the Messiah's virginal conception. E. J. Young (1965) and J. Alec Motyer (1993) point to the definite article (the almah), to the fact that the word is never clearly used of a married woman, to the solemn announcement of a sign from the Lord himself as deep as Sheol or high as heaven, and to the titles the same child receives in 8:8 and 9:6, which no ordinary child could bear. Origen (Against Celsus 1.35) and Calvin made the same argument from the word sign. Luther (1523) argued that almah fits a virgin of marriageable age better than betulah would. A second group holds a double or typological fulfillment: a child born in Ahaz's day was the immediate sign, while the name God with us and the growing portrait of chapters 8 to 11 pointed beyond him to a fuller fulfillment in Jesus. A third group stresses the way Matthew uses fulfillment, as when he applies Hosea 11:1 (a statement about Israel's exodus) to Jesus' return from Egypt in Matthew 2:15: Matthew sees in Jesus the completion of a pattern, not only the answer to a single prediction.

On the translation question, the Septuagint's parthenos was chosen by Jewish translators before Christianity existed, so the rendering cannot be blamed on Christian bias, though parthenos itself was not always technical (it is used of Dinah after she was violated, Genesis 34:3). On every Christian reading the church's confession of Jesus' virginal conception rests on the Gospel accounts (Matthew 1:18-25 and Luke 1:26-38), not on the Hebrew word alone. How directly Isaiah foresaw that conception is a question on which faithful interpreters continue to differ.

hard.q: How can a sign given to Ahaz be fulfilled seven centuries later, and did the rest of the prophecy come true?
hard.a:
The objection is that a sign is meant to be seen. Verse 11 offers Ahaz a sign he could witness, and verses 15 and 16 measure the sign by a child's early years. A birth in Bethlehem more than seven hundred years later could not have reassured or warned Ahaz, so on this view any fulfillment must lie in his own time. Medieval Jewish commentators such as Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it so, and critics from Thomas Paine to modern historical scholarship have pressed the point. Some critics add that parts of the chapter look like predictions shaped after the event, such as the sixty-five years of verse 8 and the naming of the king of Assyria in verses 17 and 20.

Those who read the verse as direct prophecy of the Messiah, including E. J. Young and J. Alec Motyer, answer that the sign is addressed to the house of David, not to Ahaz alone (the you of verses 13 and 14 is plural), and that a sign can confirm God's word after the event, as with the sign to Moses in Exodus 3:12. On their reading verses 15 and 16 use the child's infancy as a measure of time: the threat from Aram and Israel would pass before a child could reach the age of moral choice. Others, holding a near and far fulfillment, find the immediate sign in a child born in those years (some point to Maher-shalal-hash-baz in 8:3-4, whose birth is tied to the same timetable) and the far fulfillment in Jesus, the true Immanuel whom the rest of the section describes.

On the historical question, the part of the prophecy that can be checked was fulfilled quickly: Damascus fell in 732 BC and Rezin was executed, Galilee and Gilead were annexed the same year, and Samaria fell in 722 BC, all within the few years verse 16 allows. The Assyrian flood of verses 17 to 25 came under Sennacherib in 701 BC, whose annals claim forty-six of Judah's fortified cities. Scholars who hold that prophets could speak of the future and those who think some details were added later both agree that the core of the oracle, the failure of the Syro-Ephraimite coalition, fits the years in which it is set.

observe: What does Isaiah tell Ahaz to do first (verse 4), and how does he describe the two kings Ahaz fears?
Where does Isaiah meet Ahaz (verse 3), and where does the same place appear again in Isaiah 36:2?
What changes in Isaiah's words between verse 11 and verse 13, and to whom is the sign of verse 14 finally addressed?
interpret: Why is Ahaz's refusal to ask for a sign (verse 12) treated as unbelief rather than humility, when Deuteronomy 6:16 forbids testing the LORD?
